paras.text: Envelope and Interior: Insulation, Ventilation, Windows and Doors, Finishes, and Specialties

This chapter covers about fifteen questions on your trade exam: roughly five on insulation, two on ventilation, five on windows, doors, and skylights, and the rest split between interior finishes and specialty items. Everything here comes from the twenty fifteen Michigan Residential Code — not the twenty twenty-one code. Michigan amended some of these numbers away from the national defaults, and those amendments are exactly where the exam sets its traps. Let's work through it.

Start with insulation, because it carries the most weight. Michigan has three climate zones. Zone five A is the southern Lower Peninsula — Detroit, Grand Rapids, Lansing. Zone six A is the northern Lower Peninsula and the eastern Upper Peninsula. Zone seven is the western U P — the coldest part of the state.

Here is the single most important Michigan amendment in this whole chapter. In zone five A, the ceiling insulation requirement is R thirty-eight. The national energy code says R forty-nine for zone five, but Michigan amended it down to thirty-eight. So if the question says southern Michigan, or names a southern city, the answer is R thirty-eight, and R forty-nine is the trap. In zones six A and seven — northern Michigan and the U P — the ceiling is R forty-nine. Say it back to yourself: south thirty-eight, north forty-nine.

Walls are easier because they're the same statewide: R twenty in the cavity, or R thirteen cavity plus R five continuous insulated sheathing on the outside. Floors over unconditioned space are R thirty, except zone seven, where they rise to R thirty-eight. Basement walls: in zone five A you need R ten continuous or R thirteen cavity. In zones six A and seven, it's R fifteen continuous or R nineteen cavity. When you see two numbers with a slash, like ten slash thirteen, the first number is always continuous insulation — rigid foam — and the second is cavity insulation in a framed wall. Either one complies. Slab edges get R ten in every zone; the difference is depth — two feet down in zone five A, four feet down in six A and seven.

Windows tie into the energy table too. The maximum window U factor in Michigan is zero point three two, in every zone. Not zero point three zero — that's the twenty twenty-one national number and it is not in force. Skylights get zero point five five. And remember U factor runs backward from R value: lower is better, because U factor is one divided by R. One more giveaway: there is no solar heat gain requirement in Michigan. S H G C limits are for hot southern climates. If a Michigan question offers you a solar heat gain number, it's a trap — the table says not required.

Air leakage is another Michigan amendment. The maximum is four air changes per hour at fifty pascals, verified with a mandatory blower door test. The model code says three; Michigan says four. Four is your answer.

Now vapor retarders, which the exam loves because installers get them wrong in real life. In climate zones five, six, and seven — which is all of Michigan — you need a Class one or Class two vapor retarder on the interior side of frame walls. Interior means the warm-in-winter side. Class one is poly sheeting or foil facing, a tenth of a perm or less. Class two is kraft-faced batts, up to one perm. Class three is just latex paint, up to ten perms, and it's only allowed when the wall can dry — either vented cladding over the sheathing, or enough continuous insulated sheathing to keep the wall warm: R five over a two by four wall in zone five, R seven and a half over a two by six. And never, ever put poly on the outside of a Michigan wall. With the required interior retarder, that builds a double vapor barrier — moisture gets in and can't dry either direction. That's rot and mold, and it's a wrong answer every time.

A few insulation odds and ends. Fiberglass batts run about R three point two per inch, blown cellulose about three point five, extruded polystyrene about five, closed-cell spray foam six or better. Compressing a batt into a smaller cavity lowers its R value — an R nineteen squeezed into a two by four wall performs like R thirteen. And at the eaves, insulation baffles must hold a one-inch minimum air space between the insulation and the roof sheathing so ventilation air can move.

That brings us to ventilation. Attic ventilation is the one-to-one-fifty rule: net free vent area equal to one one-hundred-fiftieth of the attic floor area. You can cut that in half, to one three-hundredth, if either of two conditions is met — either a Class one or two vapor retarder on the warm side of the ceiling, which only counts in climate zones six and seven, not in zone five A, or forty to fifty percent of the vent area placed high in the attic, within three feet of the ridge measured vertically, with the rest down at the eaves. Either condition alone is enough. Quick math: a fifteen-hundred-square-foot attic at one to three hundred needs five square feet of net free area; at one to one fifty it needs ten.

Mechanical ventilation has two little numbers the exam swaps on you constantly. Bathrooms: fifty C F M intermittent, or twenty continuous. Kitchens: one hundred C F M intermittent, or twenty-five continuous. Bigger room load, bigger number — the kitchen gets a hundred. Every exhaust fan discharges outdoors. Never into the attic, never into a soffit, never into a crawl space — dumping moist air in an attic breeds mold and feeds ice dams.

And here's the connection question they like: whole-house mechanical ventilation is required whenever the blower door test comes in under five air changes per hour. Michigan requires every new house to test at four or tighter. So every new Michigan home needs whole-house mechanical ventilation. Typical rate for a house between fifteen hundred and three thousand square feet with two or three bedrooms: sixty C F M continuous.

One specialty item rides along with ventilation: radon. The E P A action level is four picocuries per liter. The standard new-construction answer is a passive sub-slab depressurization system — a four-inch gravel layer under the slab, a poly soil-gas retarder, and a three-to-four-inch vent pipe running from under the slab straight up through the roof, with power roughed in for a future fan.

Now windows and doors — five questions, and egress is the heart of it. Emergency escape and rescue openings are required in every sleeping room, in basements with habitable space, and in habitable attics. Burn these four numbers in: five point seven square feet of net clear opening — five point zero if it's a grade-floor opening. Minimum clear height twenty-four inches. Minimum clear width twenty inches. Maximum sill height forty-four inches above the floor. It must open from inside without keys, tools, or special knowledge. And here's the classic trick: a window at exactly twenty wide and twenty-four high is only three point three three square feet. Meeting both minimum dimensions does not meet the area. One dimension has to be bigger. If the egress window is below grade, the window well needs nine square feet of horizontal area with thirty-six inches in each direction, and if the well is deeper than forty-four inches, it needs a permanent ladder or steps.

Safety glazing — tempered glass — is the other big window topic, section R three oh eight point four. The hazardous locations: All glass in doors. Glass within a twenty-four-inch arc of either side of a closed door when the bottom edge is under sixty inches above the floor. Big panes that meet all four of these together: over nine square feet, bottom edge under eighteen inches from the floor, top edge over thirty-six inches, and a walking surface within thirty-six inches. Glass in guards and railings — always, no exceptions. Wet locations — any glass with a bottom edge less than sixty inches above a tub or shower drain and within sixty inches horizontally of the water. Sixty, not seventy-two. And stairways: glass within thirty-six inches horizontally of a walking surface and under sixty inches above it, plus glass within sixty inches of the bottom tread. Tempered panes carry a permanent etched label — no label, no pass.

Two more door-and-window rules. Window fall protection: if an operable window's sill is less than twenty-four inches above the floor inside, and the drop outside is more than seventy-two inches, the opening can't pass a four-inch sphere, or it needs an approved opening-control device. Every house needs at least one side-hinged exterior egress door with thirty-two inches of clear width and seventy-eight inches of clear height. And the door from an attached garage into the house: one and three-eighths inch solid wood, one and three-eighths solid or honeycomb-core steel, or a twenty-minute fire-rated door — self-closing — and it may never open into a bedroom.

On to interior finishes, which mostly means drywall. Fastener spacing without adhesive: ceilings take nails every seven inches or screws every twelve. Walls take nails every eight or screws every sixteen. Ceilings are always tighter — gravity. Screws have to bite five-eighths of an inch into the wood. Half-inch board is standard on walls and on ceilings framed sixteen inches on center. At twenty-four on center, ceilings step up to five-eighths, or half-inch sag-resistant board. Type X is the fire-rated core; Type C is the upgraded fire-rated core that outperforms X.

The garage separation is a guaranteed question somewhere on this exam. Walls between the garage and the house: half-inch gypsum on the garage side, every wall, always. The ceiling of a garage with living space above it: five-eighths Type X. Structure supporting that floor: half-inch. The trap runs both directions — Type X on the walls is wrong, and plain half-inch on a ceiling under a bedroom is wrong. And remember, this is a separation, not a rated assembly. If an answer says one-hour fire wall, that's the trap. Ducts through the separation must be twenty-six gauge steel with no openings into the garage.

Drywall finish levels, zero through five. Level one, tape embedded, for plenums. Level two, tape plus one coat, for garages and behind tile. Level three, two coats, for heavy texture. Level four, three coats, standard for flat paint. Level five adds a skim coat over the whole surface — that's for gloss, semi-gloss, and critical lighting.

Wet areas: tub and shower walls need a nonabsorbent finish to six feet above the floor. Tile in wet areas goes over cement board, fiber-cement, or glass-mat gypsum — never paper-faced green board — and it's set with thinset, the cement mortar. Mastic is for dry walls only; it softens in moisture and fails.

Last, the specialties. Attic access: required when the attic is over thirty square feet with thirty inches or more of height. The rough opening is twenty-two by thirty inches, in a hallway or other accessible spot, with thirty inches of headroom above the hatch. Memory hook: thirty, thirty, thirty, through twenty-two by thirty. Smoke alarms: in every bedroom, outside every sleeping area, on every story including the basement — all interconnected, hardwired with battery backup. Carbon monoxide alarms: the trigger is a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage; the location is outside each sleeping area; and under the twenty fifteen code they do not have to interconnect — interconnection is a smoke alarm rule. Pool barriers: forty-eight inches high, no opening passes a four-inch sphere, self-closing self-latching gate with the latch at fifty-four inches or on the pool side.

Rapid-fire recap. Ceiling insulation: R thirty-eight south, R forty-nine north. Walls: R twenty, or thirteen plus five. Basement: ten thirteen south, fifteen nineteen north. Slab: R ten, two feet south, four feet north. Window U factor: point three two. Skylight: point five five. Air leakage: four A C H fifty with a blower door test. Vapor retarder: Class one or two, interior side. Attic vents: one to one fifty, or one to three hundred. Baffle air space: one inch. Bath fan: fifty and twenty. Kitchen fan: one hundred and twenty-five. Whole house trigger: under five A C H fifty. Egress: five point seven square feet, five flat at grade, twenty-four high, twenty wide, forty-four sill. Window well: nine square feet, thirty-six inches, ladder past forty-four deep. Tempered glass: twenty-four-inch door arc under sixty; nine square feet, eighteen, thirty-six, thirty-six; sixty above the drain; thirty-six and sixty at stairs. Fall protection: sill under twenty-four in, drop over seventy-two out, four-inch sphere. Egress door: thirty-two by seventy-eight clear. Garage door to house: one and three-eighths, self-closing, never to a bedroom. Garage gypsum: half-inch walls, five-eighths Type X ceiling. Drywall fasteners: seven and twelve on ceilings, eight and sixteen on walls. Screws: five-eighths bite. Tub walls: nonabsorbent to six feet. Attic access: twenty-two by thirty, thirty square feet, thirty inches headroom. Radon: four picocuries per liter. Know these cold and this domain is yours.
